subject: History
topic: Khilji and Tughlaq dynasties — mixed tiers
description: Alauddin Khilji's reforms, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments, Firuz Shah, market reforms

questions.stem: The Khilji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1290 by:
questions.explanation: Jalaluddin Firuz Khilji — founded the Khilji dynasty 1290 CE by overthrowing the last Slave dynasty Sultan Kaiqubad. Was already 70+ when he ascended; mild ruler. Murdered by his nephew/son-in-law Alauddin (1296), who had captured Devagiri's wealth. Khilji rule (1290-1320 CE). Followed by Tughlaq dynasty (1320-1414) founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq after he overthrew Khusrau Khan (Hindu convert who killed Mubarak Shah Khilji).

questions.stem: Alauddin Khilji's most famous economic reform was:

options.option_text: Market control / price-fixing system in Delhi

questions.explanation: Alauddin Khilji (r. 1296-1316) — fixed prices of essentials in Delhi (grains, cloth, slaves, horses, cattle) for the army's benefit. Set up four markets — Mandi (grains), Sara-i-Adl (cloth), separate markets for horses/cattle and slaves. Officials: Diwan-i-Riyasat (controller), Shahna-i-Mandi (market officer), reporters (Barids, Munhiyans). Strict punishments for cheating. Token currency was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiment (later, 1329-32). Land redistribution wasn't a Khilji reform; rather, kharaj raised to 50% of produce.

questions.stem: Alauddin Khilji's slave-general who led successful Deccan campaigns and later seized the throne briefly was:
questions.explanation: Malik Kafur (Hazardinari — 'thousand-dinar slave') — Alauddin's eunuch slave-general. Led campaigns into Deccan: Devagiri (Yadavas, 1307), Warangal (Kakatiyas, 1309), Halebid (Hoysalas, 1311), Madurai (Pandyas, 1311) — the deepest reach of Delhi Sultanate into South India. Returned with vast wealth (incl. famed Koh-i-Noor diamond from Warangal). After Alauddin's death (1316), tried to seize power but was assassinated 35 days later. Ulugh Khan (Alauddin's brother), Zafar Khan, Nusrat Khan — earlier generals.

questions.stem: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's transfer of capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri) was carried out around:
questions.explanation: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325-51) — transferred capital from Delhi to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad) in 1327, ostensibly to better control the Deccan. Forced entire Delhi population to migrate ~1,500 km. The plan failed disastrously — many died on the journey, north-west frontier weakened, capital reverted to Delhi 1335. Other failed experiments: token currency in copper/brass (1329-32, leading to widespread forgery; tokens redeemed for silver, draining treasury); Khurasan and Qarachil expeditions. Ibn Battuta visited the court (1334-42).

questions.stem: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-88) is best remembered for:

options.option_text: Public works — canals, hospitals (Dar-ul-Shifa), translation bureau, abolition of cruel punishments

questions.explanation: Firuz Shah Tughlaq — successor to Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Famous for benevolent civic projects: canals (notably Western Yamuna Canal — restored & later used by British), gardens, hospitals (Dar-ul-Shifa, free medical care), employment bureau (Diwan-i-Khairat), abolition of torture and mutilation. Built four cities — Firuzabad (modern Firuz Shah Kotla, Delhi), Hissar, Fatehabad, Jaunpur. Brought TWO Ashokan pillars to Delhi (still standing — Firuz Shah Kotla and Ridge area). Firuz Shah Sultan was a Hindu mother's son; sometimes called 'Ahmed Hussain'. Restored jagirs and kept ulema close (criticised by liberal historians).

questions.stem: Timur (Tamerlane)'s sack of Delhi (1398) marked the beginning of the end of which dynasty?
questions.explanation: Timur — Turco-Mongol conqueror — sacked Delhi in December 1398 during Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq's reign. Massive massacre, plunder of treasures including Tughlaq palaces. Tughlaq dynasty officially ended 1414 — succeeded by Sayyid dynasty (1414-51) → Lodi dynasty (1451-1526) → Mughal era (Babur, 1526). Timur's invasion left Delhi devastated; food prices skyrocketed, Indo-Islamic learning largely shifted to provincial Sultanates (Jaunpur, Bengal, Kashmir, Gujarat, Malwa, Bahmani).

questions.stem: Alauddin Khilji's army system featured revolutionary measures including:

options.option_text: Branding of horses (Dagh) and descriptive rolls of soldiers (Chehra) to prevent fraud

questions.explanation: Alauddin Khilji's military reforms — first ruler to maintain a STANDING ARMY paid in CASH (not jagirs). Dagh (branding) — every horse branded with the state's mark to prevent substitution. Chehra (descriptive roll) — physical description of every soldier kept on file to prevent impersonation/proxy. These were later adopted by Sher Shah Suri and the Mughals (Akbar's mansabdari). The cash-paid army required Alauddin's market-control reforms — fixed low prices meant cash salary went further.
